questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis that appeared 3 weeks ago. On examination, the base is clean and there is non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy reveals motile spirochetes. Which statement best describes the histopathology of this lesion?
opts: Epidermal ulceration with neutrophilic infiltrate and no vascular changes
Plasma cell-rich infiltrate, endothelial swelling, and obliterative endarteritis
Caseous necrosis with Langhans giant cells and epithelioid granulomas
Acantholysis with dyskeratosis and corps ronds in the spinous layer
questions.exp: Primary syphilitic chancre shows a characteristic triad of plasma cell infiltration, endothelial swelling (Virchow's triad), and obliterative endarteritis (endarteritis obliterans) on histopathology. This reflects the host response to Treponema pallidum.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with multiple well-demarcated, violaceous plaques on the face and lower extremities. Skin biopsy shows vascular proliferation with spindle cells and slit-like spaces containing erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Advanced AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma (CD4 <200, extensive cutaneous involvement) requires systemic therapy. Liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil) is the first-line systemic agent. Antiretroviral therapy is also essential for immune reconstitution.

questions.q: A 22-year-old student presents with erythematous, scaly plaques in the scalp and beard area with yellowish greasy scale. Scraping with a blade produces a 'dandruff' appearance. KOH examination is negative. Which organism is implicated in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.exp: Seborrheic dermatitis is associated with Malassezia furfur (a lipophilic yeast). While the KOH may be negative due to low fungal load, Malassezia triggers an inflammatory response through free fatty acid production. Treatment includes ketoconazole shampoo or topical antifungals.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of erythematous plaques with silvery scales on elbows and knees. She now develops joint pain predominantly involving the DIP joints. Nail examination shows pitting and onycholysis. Her serum rheumatoid factor is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Rheumatoid arthritis with psoriasiform drug reaction
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis presents in 5-30% of psoriasis patients. DIP joint involvement, nail changes (pitting, onycholysis), and seronegative arthritis in a patient with existing psoriatic plaques strongly suggests psoriatic arthritis. It is seronegative (RF negative) unlike rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with a slowly growing warty plaque on the dorsum of the foot, present for 2 years. It shows 'black dots' on its surface and verrucous surface. Biopsy reveals thick-walled, muriform (sclerotic) bodies in the dermis. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused most commonly by Fonsecaea pedrosoi in India. Histopathology shows characteristic 'Medlar bodies' or muriform/sclerotic bodies (copper-penny bodies) — thick-walled, dark brown, septate cells. Black dots visible clinically represent transepidermal elimination of organisms.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with rapidly progressive, bilateral, symmetrical cutaneous necrosis of the breast, thighs, and buttocks 3 days after starting warfarin for DVT. Laboratory tests show protein C deficiency. What is the pathophysiology of this complication?
opts: Rapid depletion of protein C causing a transient hypercoagulable state
Direct toxic effect of warfarin on dermal vasculature
questions.exp: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis occurs due to rapid depletion of protein C (short half-life of 6-8h) before factors II, IX, X are adequately suppressed, creating a transient hypercoagulable state with microvascular thrombosis. Risk is highest with protein C or S deficiency. Affects fat-rich areas (breast, buttocks, thighs).

questions.q: A 19-year-old college student presents with multiple painful genital ulcers, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, and fever. The ulcers are soft, have undermined edges, and a dirty gray base. Gram stain of the ulcer base shows 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern. What is the recommended treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: This describes chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi). The Gram stain showing 'school of fish' arrangement is classic. Treatment options include azithromycin 1g single dose, ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose, ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 3 days, or erythromycin 500 mg TDS × 7 days. Single-dose azithromycin is preferred for compliance.

questions.q: A 40-year-old leprosy patient on MDT for 6 months presents with fever, erythema nodosum-like nodules, and acute iridocyclitis. His BIs have been decreasing. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Increase dose of dapsone and continue MDT
Thalidomide 100 mg TID and discontinue MDT
Clofazimine 300 mg loading dose and stop rifampicin
questions.exp: This is Type 2 lepra reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum - ENL), which occurs in lepromatous or borderline lepromatous leprosy. Severe ENL with iridocyclitis requires systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 40-60 mg/day tapered). MDT must be continued. Thalidomide is reserved for recurrent severe ENL where steroids are contraindicated.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 3-year history of recurrent oral ulcers, acneiform lesions, and arthralgia. She now develops pathergy — a papule forming at a needle prick site. Fundoscopy shows posterior uveitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease (silk road disease) is characterized by the triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and ocular inflammation (uveitis). Pathergy (positive pathergy test — papule formation at needle prick site) is highly specific. Acneiform lesions and arthralgia are also common features.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with multiple flaccid bullae that rupture easily leaving raw erosions on trunk, limbs, and oral mucosa. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG and C3 deposits in an intercellular 'fish-net' pattern. The target antigen is on the keratinocyte surface. Diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris shows flaccid bullae, Nikolsky sign positive, mucosal involvement. DIF shows IgG+C3 in intercellular spaces (fish-net/chicken-wire pattern). The target antigen is Desmoglein-3 (mucocutaneous) or Desmoglein-1+3 (mucocutaneous). Bullous pemphigoid targets BP180/BP230 at the DEJ.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with a history of SLE presents with a photo-distributed rash showing annular, polycyclic, scaly plaques on sun-exposed areas. ANA is positive (1:320). Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies are elevated. What subtype of cutaneous lupus does she have?
questions.exp: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) presents with photo-distributed annular/polycyclic or papulosquamous plaques. It is strongly associated with anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (>80% of cases). SCLE does not cause scarring (unlike DLE) and has less systemic involvement than acute CLE (malar rash).

questions.q: A newborn presents on day 2 of life with erythematous macules, papules, and vesicles containing eosinophils on Wright stain. The palms and soles are spared. The lesions begin to resolve spontaneously by 2 weeks. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN) presents in 30-70% of term neonates with erythematous macules/papules/vesicles sparing palms/soles. Wright stain shows eosinophils. Self-resolving by 1-2 weeks. Staphylococcal pustulosis shows neutrophils. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is more common in dark-skinned neonates and shows neutrophils.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man develops a pearly, translucent, telangiectatic nodule on his nose that has been slowly enlarging over 2 years. Biopsy reveals basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, retraction artifact, and fibromyxoid stroma. What is the most important treatment consideration?
opts: Wide local excision with 2 cm margins
Mohs micrographic surgery for the nose location due to high recurrence risk
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose (H-zone of the face) is high-risk for recurrence due to location near critical structures. Mohs micrographic surgery is the preferred treatment for high-risk locations (nose, periorbital, periauricular) as it offers the highest cure rates with maximal tissue preservation. The H-zone has highest recurrence risk.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a firm, skin-colored nodule on his thigh present for 1 year. It is mildly tender, dimples inward on lateral compression (dimple sign positive). Histology shows a storiform pattern of spindle cells with hemosiderin deposits and mild lymphocytic infiltrate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatofibroma (DFH/BFH) presents as a firm, slightly tender nodule with a positive Fitzpatrick dimple sign (dimpling on lateral compression). Histology shows storiform pattern of fibroblasts/histiocytes, hemosiderin, and overlying epidermal hyperplasia. DFSP also has a storiform pattern but shows honeycomb fat infiltration and CD34 positivity.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman undergoing treatment for borderline tuberculoid leprosy develops sudden wrist drop, a lagophthalmos, and extreme tenderness over the right ulnar nerve. Her skin lesions become erythematous and edematous. What is happening and what is the immediate management?
opts: Type 1 lepra reaction; restart multidrug therapy with corticosteroids
Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction); systemic corticosteroids 40-60 mg/day and continue MDT
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurs in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL). Features include erythema/edema of existing skin lesions, acute neuritis causing functional loss (wrist drop, lagophthalmos). Management: systemic prednisolone 40-60 mg/day tapered over 6 months and continue MDT. Nerve decompression may be needed for severe neuritis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the lower lip, recurring every 6-8 weeks, usually triggered by sunlight. Tzanck smear shows multinucleate giant cells. What is the most effective prophylactic treatment?
opts: Topical acyclovir 5% cream applied at onset of prodrome only
Daily suppressive oral acyclovir 400 mg BD
Oral valacyclovir 2g single dose at prodrome onset
questions.exp: Recurrent herpes labialis (HSV-1) with frequent episodes (>6/year) benefits from daily suppressive therapy with oral acyclovir 400 mg BD or valacyclovir 500 mg OD. Suppressive therapy reduces frequency by 70-80%. Episodic therapy at prodrome (valacyclovir 2g BD × 1 day) reduces duration but does not prevent recurrences.

questions.q: A 60-year-old diabetic man presents with painful erythema and swelling of the scrotum that rapidly progressed over 48 hours with crepitus on palpation and systemic toxicity. CT scan shows gas in the fascial planes. What is the most important first step in management?
opts: High-dose IV antibiotics covering polymicrobial flora
Immediate surgical debridement combined with IV antibiotics
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as primary treatment
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum — a surgical emergency. The cornerstone of treatment is aggressive and immediate surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue, combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering polymicrobial (gram-positive, gram-negative, anaerobes). Surgery cannot be delayed — antibiotics alone are insufficient.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a slowly expanding plaque on the trunk with a raised, thread-like border and central clearing. Wood's lamp examination shows coral-pink fluorescence in the active border. Scrapings show hyphae and arthrospores on KOH. What causes this fluorescence?
opts: Pteridine metabolites produced by Microsporum canis
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UV) shows bright green/yellow-green fluorescence in Microsporum infections (Microsporum canis, M. audouinii) due to pteridine metabolites. Trichophyton species generally do not fluoresce. Coral-pink/brick-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp is characteristic of erythrasma (Corynebacterium minutissimum), not dermatophytes.

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman presents with pruritic papules and burrows between the fingers, on the wrist flexures, and periareolar area. Her husband has similar symptoms. Dermoscopy reveals the 'jet with contrail' sign. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Topical lindane 1% lotion applied once to the whole body
Topical permethrin 5% cream applied from neck down, left for 8-12 hours, single application
Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg single dose only
Topical benzyl benzoate 25% once weekly for 4 weeks
questions.exp: Scabies treatment of choice is topical permethrin 5% cream applied from neck down for 8-12 hours. A second application 1 week later is recommended. All household contacts should be treated simultaneously. Oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg) is an alternative, particularly for crusted scabies, immunocompromised patients, or when topical therapy fails. Lindane is avoided due to neurotoxicity.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with indurated, erythematous plaques on the shins bilaterally, present for 2 months. She recently had a sore throat. Biopsy shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis. ASO titres are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum (EN) presents as tender, bilateral, erythematous nodules/plaques on the shins, often after a streptococcal throat infection. Histology shows septal panniculitis WITHOUT vasculitis (Miescher's granulomas). Nodular vasculitis/erythema induratum shows lobular panniculitis WITH vasculitis, often associated with TB.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, raised, non-tender inguinal mass that has been slowly enlarging for 3 months. No genital ulcers are seen. Biopsy of the groin mass shows 'donovan bodies' — encapsulated bipolar staining rods within macrophages on Giemsa stain. What is the appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 weeks
Azithromycin 1g orally once weekly for at least 3 weeks
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis shows Donovan bodies on Giemsa stain. WHO and CDC first-line treatment is azithromycin 1g weekly (or 500 mg daily) for at least 3 weeks and until lesions heal. Doxycycline 100 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks is an alternative.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops tense, subepidermal bullae predominantly on the trunk and inner thighs, with mild oral involvement. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. ELISA confirms antibodies against BP180 (collagen XVII). What is the first-line treatment?
opts: Superpotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol 0.05%) for mild-moderate disease or oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day with adjuvant for severe disease
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) first-line for mild-moderate disease is superpotent topical steroids (clobetasol propionate 0.05%) which is as effective as systemic steroids with fewer side effects. For severe/generalized disease, oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day with adjuvants (doxycycline+nicotinamide, dapsone, or immunosuppressants) is used.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man presents with a slowly growing, painless mass on his scalp. It is a firm, yellow-white, multilobulated subcutaneous nodule. Histology shows a cyst with a granular layer lacking (no stratum granulosum), filled with homogeneous eosinophilic material. What is this lesion?
questions.exp: Trichilemmal (pilar) cyst occurs most commonly on the scalp (90%). Histologically, it lacks a granular layer (unlike epidermoid cysts which have a prominent granular layer) and contains homogeneous, compact keratinous material resembling the outer root sheath epithelium. They are often multiple and may have autosomal dominant inheritance.

questions.q: During patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis, a patient shows a ++ reaction (erythema, infiltration, discrete vesicles) at day 4 but not day 2. What is the significance of a reading only at day 4 but not at day 2?
opts: This indicates an irritant reaction that develops late
This indicates a late-positive reaction to some allergens like neomycin, corticosteroids, or metals
The reaction should be considered negative as it peaked after day 2
questions.exp: Some allergens characteristically cause late reactions in patch testing appearing at D4-D7 but not D2. These include neomycin, corticosteroids (especially budesonide), certain metals (gold), formaldehyde releasers, and some rubber chemicals. Reading only at D2 would miss these late positives. Standard readings are at D2 (48h) and D4 or D7.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with discrete hypopigmented macules on the trunk following a vesicular eruption 6 months ago. The vesicles had been arranged in linear bands following dermatomal distribution. The current macules are also in the same dermatomal pattern. What is this condition?
questions.exp: Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation following herpes zoster is well-recognized. The dermatomal vesicular eruption (zoster) causes post-inflammatory changes including hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation in the affected dermatome. The distribution follows the original rash. This is different from vitiligo which is not confined to dermatomes.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with diffuse, non-inflammatory follicular hyperkeratosis on the extensor aspects of his upper arms and thighs, giving a rough 'chicken skin' texture. His mother has similar skin. What is the underlying pathology?
opts: Deficiency of filaggrin leading to impaired epidermal barrier
Retention hyperkeratosis of hair follicles due to abnormal cornification
Inflammatory infiltrate around hair follicles causing scarring
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the dermis
questions.exp: Keratosis pilaris (KP) is caused by abnormal follicular cornification (retention hyperkeratosis) where keratin plugs accumulate within hair follicle infundibuli. It is often associated with atopy, ichthyosis vulgaris, and filaggrin mutations. Filaggrin mutation is a risk factor but not the direct pathology — the primary defect is abnormal keratinization of the follicular epithelium.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a punch biopsy on a suspicious lesion. The specimen is oriented with the epidermis facing up and placed in 10% neutral buffered formalin. For direct immunofluorescence (DIF), the tissue should be placed in which transport medium?
questions.exp: For direct immunofluorescence (DIF), tissue must be sent in Michel's transport medium (containing ammonium sulfate), which preserves immunoreactants at room temperature for up to 2 weeks. Formalin destroys immunoglobulins and complement. Saline is used only for short transport (<4h) to a cryostat. Glutaraldehyde is for electron microscopy.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with multiple, discrete, firm, skin-colored nodules along the course of peripheral nerves. He has café-au-lait macules (>10), axillary freckling, and Lisch nodules on slit-lamp examination. What gene is mutated in this condition?
opts: TSC1 or TSC2 (tuberin/hamartin) on chromosomes 9 and 16
questions.exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1/von Recklinghausen disease) is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene encoding neurofibromin on chromosome 17q11.2, a tumor suppressor (RAS-GAP). Diagnostic criteria include ≥6 café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas, optic glioma, and positive family history.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with symmetric hyperpigmentation on the malar area, forehead, and upper lip that worsens with sun exposure. She has been taking OCP for 5 years. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of the pigmentation. What does enhancement on Wood's lamp indicate?
opts: Dermal pigmentation — poor response to topical therapy
Epidermal pigmentation — better response to topical depigmenting agents
questions.exp: In melasma, Wood's lamp examination helps classify the pattern. Enhancement (accentuation) of pigmentation under Wood's lamp indicates epidermal melanin, which responds better to topical therapy (hydroquinone, retinoids, chemical peels). Non-enhancement suggests dermal melanin, which is recalcitrant to treatment. Mixed pattern shows partial enhancement.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman presents with pruritic, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows subepidermal vesicle with neutrophilic infiltrate at the dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. She has a malabsorption syndrome. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces, associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF shows granular IgA at the DEJ (pathognomonic). Treatment is dapsone for rapid symptom control plus a strict gluten-free diet for long-term remission. Diet allows gradual reduction of dapsone over years.

questions.q: A physician is treating a patient with moderate-severe psoriasis using methotrexate (MTX). After 1.5 g cumulative dose, a liver biopsy is recommended. Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to methotrexate therapy in psoriasis?
questions.exp: Methotrexate contraindications include hepatic disease, alcoholism (>14 units/week), renal impairment (GFR <50 mL/min), active infections (hepatitis, TB), pregnancy, breastfeeding, and severe bone marrow suppression. Well-controlled hypertension on a calcium channel blocker is NOT a contraindication to MTX. Note: amlodipine does not significantly interact with MTX.
